_meta.note: General organic / sustainable practices summarised from public extension guidance, for demonstration only. No doses are prescribed: quantities depend on soil test, crop and local recommendation. Use certified inputs and follow product labels and your organic certification standard. To be replaced by the verified Kisan Drishti organic dataset.

items.name: Vermicompost
items.summary: Earthworm-processed compost that adds organic matter and slowly releases nutrients.
howTo: Use well-matured vermicompost (dark, earthy smell, no heat)
Apply at field preparation, or place near rows in standing crop and lightly incorporate
Irrigate lightly afterwards so it contacts moist soil
items.timing: Best at field preparation; small top-ups possible in standing crop.
cautions: Nutrient content varies by batch — it works slowly and may not correct a severe deficiency on its own

items.name: Farmyard manure (FYM)
items.summary: Well-decomposed cattle dung and bedding — builds organic carbon and supplies nutrients over time.
howTo: Use only fully decomposed manure
Spread evenly before the last ploughing and mix into the soil
items.timing: Before sowing. Plan it for the next season if the crop is already standing.
cautions: Fresh manure can carry weed seeds and pathogens and may temporarily lock up nitrogen

items.name: Azotobacter biofertilizer
items.summary: Free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria used for non-legume crops such as wheat, maize and mustard.
howTo: Use a certified product within its expiry date
Seed treatment before sowing, or mix with well-decomposed compost and apply to moist soil in the standing crop
Keep away from direct sun and from chemical seed treatments
items.timing: Seed treatment at sowing; soil application with compost in standing crop.
cautions: Supplements but does not replace a full nutrient plan — effect depends on soil organic matter and moisture

items.name: Rhizobium inoculant
items.summary: Crop-specific bacteria that help legumes such as chickpea form nitrogen-fixing root nodules.
howTo: Use the strain specific to the legume crop
Treat seed in shade just before sowing
cautions: Must match the crop — a strain for another legume will not work

items.name: Phosphate-solubilising bacteria (PSB)
items.summary: Helps release soil phosphorus that roots cannot otherwise access.
howTo: Seed treatment, or mix with compost and apply to moist soil
Can be combined with Azotobacter
items.timing: At sowing or early in the season.
cautions: Works on phosphorus already present in the soil — does not add phosphorus

items.name: Potash-mobilising bacteria (KSB)
items.summary: Helps make soil potassium more available to the crop.
howTo: Apply with compost to moist soil or as seed treatment
items.timing: At sowing or early in the season.

items.name: Enriched compost for micronutrients
items.summary: Compost prepared or enriched with materials allowed under organic standards to help micronutrient supply.
howTo: Check which enrichment materials your certification standard permits
Apply matured compost at field preparation
cautions: Confirm the deficiency with a repeat soil or plant test before relying on it

items.name: Green manuring (e.g. dhaincha, sunhemp)
items.summary: Grow a fast legume and turn it into the soil before flowering to add organic matter and nitrogen.
howTo: Sow in the gap between main crops (for wheat–rice systems, the summer window)
Incorporate at about 40–50 days, before it becomes woody
Allow some time to decompose before the next sowing
items.timing: Between seasons — plan it for after this harvest.
cautions: Needs water and a free field window; not possible in a standing crop
items.evidence: General extension guidance; dhaincha is commonly used on alkaline soils

items.name: Crop-residue mulching
items.summary: Keep residue on the surface instead of burning it — conserves moisture and slowly builds organic carbon.
howTo: Retain chopped residue on the surface
Avoid residue burning
items.timing: After harvest or between rows in wide-spaced crops.
cautions: Very thick mulch can shelter pests in some crops

items.name: Rotate with a legume
items.summary: Include a pulse (e.g. moong, chickpea) in the rotation to add nitrogen and break pest and disease cycles.
howTo: Plan the next season's crop around a legume
A short summer moong between wheat and the next crop is a common option
cautions: Choose a legume suited to your soil and water availability

items.name: Rust-preventive field practices
items.summary: Resistant varieties, balanced nitrogen, regular scouting and early reporting — the backbone of rust management.
howTo: Scout twice a week while cool, humid weather lasts
Avoid extra nitrogen top-dressing during high-risk spells
Report confirmed patches early to your local agriculture officer / KVK
items.timing: Now — while conditions are favourable for rust.
cautions: If rust is confirmed and spreading, ask local experts which control options your certification allows

items.name: Canopy management for mildew
items.summary: Moderate sowing density and balanced nutrition keep the canopy airy and less favourable to mildew.
howTo: Note dense, shaded patches during scouting
Plan seed rate and row spacing for next season

items.name: Yellow sticky traps
items.summary: Simple traps that show when flying aphids arrive, so you act on evidence rather than calendar spraying.
howTo: Place a few traps at crop-canopy height across the field
Check and record counts twice a week
cautions: Traps are for monitoring — they do not control an established infestation

items.name: Conserve natural enemies
items.summary: Ladybird beetles, lacewings and hoverflies feed on aphids. Protecting them is the first line of defence.
howTo: Avoid broad-spectrum sprays
Keep flowering border plants where practical
Count natural enemies when scouting

items.name: Neem-based botanical preparation
items.summary: A permitted botanical option for soft-bodied pests such as aphids, used only when monitoring shows it is needed.
howTo: Use a certified, labelled product and follow the label
Spray only if counts cross the local threshold advised by experts
Spray in the evening to protect pollinators
cautions: Botanicals can also harm beneficial insects — not a routine spray
Check your organic certification's permitted-input list

items.name: Trichoderma bio-agent
items.summary: A beneficial fungus used as seed or soil treatment against some soil-borne diseases. It is not a rust treatment.
howTo: Seed treatment, or multiply in well-decomposed FYM before soil application
Use a certified product
